# R basics {.divider background-color="#8C0014"}

::: {.kicker}
Before we start
:::

Objects · functions · vectors · data frames · lists

## Objects, functions and packages

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="on">Setup</span><span>1 · dplyr</span><span>2 · tidyr</span><span>3 · purrr</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="48%"}
```r
x <- 5          # store 5 as object x
x * 2           # returns 10

round(3.14159, digits = 2)
                # function: returns 3.14

library("dplyr")  # load a package
?round            # open the help page
```
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.card .compact}
[Object]{.ct}
A named value stored in memory. `<-` assigns: it creates or overwrites the object. Nothing is kept unless you assign it.
:::

::: {.card .compact}
[Function and arguments]{.ct}
A function takes inputs, called **arguments**, inside `( )` and returns an output. Arguments can be named: `digits = 2`.
:::

::: {.card .compact}
[Package]{.ct}
A collection of functions written by others. Install once with `install.packages()`, load in every session with `library()`.
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: R basics, 7 minutes across this slide and the next two. Type the examples into the console live.

- An object is anything with a name. If you run code without `<-`, R prints the result and then forgets it.
- Functions always have brackets. Inside the brackets go the arguments. `?` followed by a function name opens the documentation, which lists every argument.
- Names are case-sensitive: `X` and `x` are different objects.
:::

## Vectors, data frames and lists

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="on">Setup</span><span>1 · dplyr</span><span>2 · tidyr</span><span>3 · purrr</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="structs">
  <div class="struct">
    <span class="sname">Vector</span>
    <div class="vec"><i>39.5</i><i>49.3</i><i>56.3</i></div>
    <code>c(39.5, 49.3, 56.3)</code>
    <span class="sdesc">Several values of <b>one type</b> in a sequence. <code>c()</code> combines values into a vector.</span>
  </div>
  <div class="struct">
    <span class="sname">Data frame · tibble</span>
    <div class="df2"><b>country</b><b>lifeexp</b><i>Niger</i><i>57.1</i><i>Honduras</i><i>69.8</i><i>Suriname</i><i>69.6</i></div>
    <code>tibble(country = ..., lifeexp = ...)</code>
    <span class="sdesc">A table. Each <b>column</b> is a vector, all of the same length. Rows are observations, columns are variables. A tibble is a data frame that prints more neatly.</span>
  </div>
  <div class="struct">
    <span class="sname">List</span>
    <div class="lst"><i>a data frame</i><i>a vector</i><i>another data frame</i></div>
    <code>list(df1, x, df2)</code>
    <span class="sdesc">A container whose <b>elements</b> can be any kind of object, of any length. Used in Part 3.</span>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
- Almost everything in R is a vector. A single number is a vector of length 1.
- A data frame is a set of vectors of equal length, side by side. `df$lifeexp` extracts one column as a vector.
- A list can hold different kinds of objects. Part 3 works with a list of data frames.
:::

## Types, missing values and comparisons

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="on">Setup</span><span>1 · dplyr</span><span>2 · tidyr</span><span>3 · purrr</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
| Type | Example | Note |
|---|---|---|
| numeric | `57.1` | numbers |
| character | `"Niger"` | text, always in quotes |
| logical | `TRUE`, `FALSE` | results of comparisons |
| missing | `NA` | value not available |

::: {.source-note}
`"1970"` in quotes is text, not a number. `class()` tells you the type.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
| Operator | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `==` | equal to | `year == 1990` |
| `!=` | not equal to | `design != "Experiment"` |
| `>` `<` | greater, less than | `n > 100` |
| `%in%` | is one of | `year %in% c(1970, 1990)` |
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
- `=` sets an argument; `==` tests whether two things are equal. Mixing them up is one of the most common errors.
- `%in%` checks each value against a vector of allowed values. We use it in Part 2 to keep several countries and years.
- `NA` is R's code for a missing value. Most calculations involving `NA` return `NA`.
:::

# Summarising data with dplyr {.divider background-color="#8C0014"}

::: {.kicker}
Part 1
:::

`count()` · `mutate()` · `group_by()` · `summarise()`

## Inspecting a data set

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Setup</span><span class="on">1 · dplyr</span><span>2 · tidyr</span><span>3 · purrr</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="52%"}
```r
?agadullina2018          # documentation
class(agadullina2018)    # "data.frame"

agadullina2018_tbl <- as_tibble(agadullina2018)
agadullina2018_tbl       # prints 10 rows + types
glimpse(agadullina2018_tbl)
```
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.card}
[Data]{.ct}
A meta-analysis: **85 effect sizes** from 21 studies on out-group entitativity and prejudice. An effect size measures the strength of a relationship on a common scale.
:::

::: {.card .line}
[Key variables]{.ct}
`yi` is the effect size (Fisher's z), `vi` is its variance
:::
:::

::::

::: {.source-note}
Exam tip: never print a whole data frame. Use the tibble print or `glimpse()`.
:::

::: {.notes}
Timing: teaching moment 1 is about 7 minutes across this slide and the next three. Live-code it if you can.

- The first thing to do with any new dataset is to find out what it is: `?` gives the documentation, and `class()` gives the type.
- Each row is an effect size from a published study. `yi` is the effect size and `vi` its variance.
- Tibbles are data frames with better manners: they print only the first rows, show column types, and never silently convert strings.
:::

## The pipe operator `|>`

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Setup</span><span class="on">1 · dplyr</span><span>2 · tidyr</span><span>3 · purrr</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

::: {.cards .c2}
::: {.card .line}
[Nested]{.ct}

```r
mutate(count(agadullina2018_tbl, design),
       pct = n / sum(n) * 100)
```

<span class="foot">Read from the inside out</span>
:::

::: {.card}
[Piped]{.ct}

```r
agadullina2018_tbl |>
  count(design) |>
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n) * 100)
```

<span class="foot">Read top to bottom: each step passes its result to the next</span>
:::
:::

::: {.source-note}
Keyboard shortcut: Ctrl + Shift + M (Windows), Cmd + Shift + M (Mac).
:::

::: {.notes}
- The pipe takes what's on the left and feeds it in as the first argument on the right.
- With one step it makes no difference. With three or more, it lets you read code like a recipe.
- We use the native `|>`. You'll see `%>%` online; for today they do the same thing. If the shortcut gives `%>%`, tick "Use native pipe operator" in RStudio's Global Options under Code.
:::

## Core `dplyr` verbs

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Setup</span><span class="on">1 · dplyr</span><span>2 · tidyr</span><span>3 · purrr</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

::: {.cards .c5}
::: {.card}
[count]{.ct}
How often does each value appear?

<span class="foot">`count(design)`</span>
:::

::: {.card}
[mutate]{.ct}
Add or change a column

<span class="foot">`mutate(pct = ...)`</span>
:::

::: {.card}
[summarise]{.ct}
Collapse many rows into one

<span class="foot">`summarise(yi = mean(yi))`</span>
:::

::: {.card .dark}
[group_by]{.ct}
Do the next step once per group

<span class="foot">`group_by(design)`</span>
:::

::: {.card}
[filter · select]{.ct}
Keep some rows · keep some columns

<span class="foot">`filter(n > 100)`</span>
:::
:::

Each verb takes a data frame as its first argument and returns a data frame.

## Grouped summaries with `group_by()`

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Setup</span><span class="on">1 · dplyr</span><span>2 · tidyr</span><span>3 · purrr</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
```r
agadullina2018_tbl |>
  summarise(yi = mean(yi))
```

```{=html}
<table class="mini"><tr><th>yi</th></tr><tr><td class="hl">0.409</td></tr></table>
<p class="tbl-cap">One row <small>for the whole data set</small></p>
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```r
agadullina2018_tbl |>
  group_by(design) |>
  summarise(yi = mean(yi))
```

```{=html}
<table class="mini"><tr><th>design</th><th>yi</th></tr><tr><td>Cross-sectional</td><td class="hl">0.468</td></tr><tr><td>Experiment</td><td class="hl">0.111</td></tr></table>
<p class="tbl-cap">One row per group <small>same code, one extra line</small></p>
```
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
- Demonstrate live: `summarise` gives one number. Add `group_by(design)` before it and you get one number per design.
- Key idea: `group_by` changes nothing visible on its own. It changes how the *next* verb behaves.
- Hand over: "Work through Part 1 in pairs. You have 16 minutes. The timer is on the next slide."
:::

```{=html}
<div class="timer" data-minutes="16"></div>
```

:::: {.yt}

::: {.tasks}
[Part 1 · notebook Q1–11]{.lbl}

1. `?agadullina2018`: read the documentation
2. `class()`: what kind of object is it?
3. Print it (just this once)
4. `as_tibble()` with a new name, then print
5. `count()` the frequencies of `design`
6. Rewrite step 5 with a pipe `|>`
7. Pipe into `mutate()`: add a percentage column
8. `summarise()` the mean of `yi`
9. Add `group_by(design)` before `summarise()`
10. What have we found out?
:::

::: {.cheat}
[Syntax you need]{.lbl}

```r
df_tbl <- as_tibble(df)          # assign with <-

df_tbl |>
  count(design) |>               # n per group
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n) * 100) # new column

df_tbl |>
  group_by(design) |>            # per group...
  summarise(yi = mean(yi))       # ...one row each
```

::: {.stuck}
**Stuck?**

- *object not found*: did you run the line with `<-`?
- *could not find function*: run the setup chunk
- Only one row? You forgot `group_by()`
- Done early? Try `glimpse()`, or `filter(n > 200)` first
:::
:::

## Part 1: results

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Setup</span><span class="on">1 · dplyr</span><span>2 · tidyr</span><span>3 · purrr</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{=html}
<p class="tbl-cap">How many effect sizes per design?</p>
<div class="bars">
  <div><span>Cross-sectional</span><i class="hot" style="width:84%"></i><b>71 · 84%</b></div>
  <div><span>Experiment</span><i style="width:16%"></i><b>14 · 16%</b></div>
</div>
<p class="tbl-cap" style="margin-top:1.2em">Mean effect size (<code>yi</code>)</p>
<div class="bars">
  <div><span>Cross-sectional</span><i class="hot" style="width:94%"></i><b>0.468</b></div>
  <div><span>Experiment</span><i style="width:22%"></i><b>0.111</b></div>
</div>
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.card}
[Result]{.ct}
84% of effect sizes come from cross-sectional designs, which report a larger mean effect than experiments (0.468 vs 0.111)
:::

::: {.card .line}
[Caveat]{.ct}
An unweighted mean gives every effect size equal weight. Meta-analytic estimates weight by precision (`vi`), covered later in the course.
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Debrief, 2–3 minutes.

- Ask 2–3 pairs: which design has the larger average effect? Why might correlational designs show bigger effects than experiments?
- Is a simple mean of `yi` the right summary? No, because it ignores precision. This is a hook for later weeks.
:::

# Tidy data and reshaping {.divider background-color="#8C0014"}

::: {.kicker}
Part 2
:::

`pivot_longer()` · `pivot_wider()` · `parse_number()`

## Tidy data

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Setup</span><span class="done">1 · dplyr</span><span class="on">2 · tidyr</span><span>3 · purrr</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

::: {.cards .c3}
::: {.card}
[1 · Variables are columns]{.ct}
Country, year and life expectancy each get their own column
:::

::: {.card}
[2 · Observations are rows]{.ct}
One row = one country in one year
:::

::: {.card}
[3 · Values are cells]{.ct}
One number per cell, nothing hidden in the headers
:::
:::

Most tidyverse functions expect data in this format.

::: {.notes}
Timing: teaching moment 2 is about 7 minutes across this slide and the next three.

- The World Bank file is a classic example of "human-friendly" data: easy to read, hard to analyse.
- Tidy data is the format that `filter`, `group_by` and `ggplot` expect.
:::

## Wide and long formats

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Setup</span><span class="done">1 · dplyr</span><span class="on">2 · tidyr</span><span>3 · purrr</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="48%"}
```{=html}
<p class="tbl-cap">Wide <small>263 rows × 67 columns</small></p>
<table class="mini">
<tr><th>country_name</th><th class="hl">1970</th><th class="hl">1990</th><th class="hl">2010</th><th>…</th></tr>
<tr><td>Burkina Faso</td><td>39.5</td><td>49.3</td><td>56.3</td><td>…</td></tr>
<tr><td>Honduras</td><td>54.4</td><td>65.2</td><td>69.8</td><td>…</td></tr>
<tr><td>Niger</td><td>35.9</td><td>41.7</td><td>57.1</td><td>…</td></tr>
</table>
```

::: {.card .err .compact}
**Year** is a variable, but it's stuck in the headers. You can't `filter(year == 1990)`.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
```{=html}
<p class="tbl-cap">Long (tidy) <small>17,358 rows × 3 columns</small></p>
<table class="mini">
<tr><th>country_name</th><th class="hl">year</th><th>lifeexp</th></tr>
<tr><td>Burkina Faso</td><td class="hl">1970</td><td>39.5</td></tr>
<tr><td>Burkina Faso</td><td class="hl">1990</td><td>49.3</td></tr>
<tr><td>Burkina Faso</td><td class="hl">2010</td><td>56.3</td></tr>
<tr><td>Honduras</td><td class="hl">1970</td><td>54.4</td></tr>
<tr><td>…</td><td>…</td><td>…</td></tr>
</table>
```
:::

::::

Wide format suits presentation tables; long format suits analysis.

::: {.notes}
- One row per country, one column per year. Year is a variable, but here it's hidden in the column names.
- Long format has one row per country-year, so you can filter by year, group by year, or plot over time.
:::

## Reshaping with `pivot_longer()` and `pivot_wider()`

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Setup</span><span class="done">1 · dplyr</span><span class="on">2 · tidyr</span><span>3 · purrr</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```r
lifeexp |>
  pivot_longer(-country_name,          # 1. which columns to stack? all but country
               names_to  = "year",     # 2. where do the old headers go?
               values_to = "lifeexp") |>  # 3. where do the numbers go?
  mutate(year = parse_number(year))    # "1970" (text) -> 1970 (number)
```

::: {.cards .c2}
::: {.card}
[`pivot_longer()`]{.ct}
Wide → long, for analysis
:::

::: {.card .dark}
[`pivot_wider()`]{.ct}
Long → wide, for a results table: `names_from = year, values_from = lifeexp`
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- `pivot_longer` asks three questions: which columns get stacked (everything except the country), where the old column names go, and where the values go.
- After pivoting, `year` is text ("1960"). `parse_number()` turns it into a number.
- `pivot_wider` reverses it.
:::

## Data quality issues in the World Bank file

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Setup</span><span class="done">1 · dplyr</span><span class="on">2 · tidyr</span><span>3 · purrr</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

::: {.cards .c2}
::: {.card .err}
[Aggregates]{.ct}

About 46 rows are regional or income-group **aggregates** ("World", "High income", "Euro area").

<span class="foot">Exclude them before averaging across countries.</span>
:::

::: {.card .err}
[Empty column]{.ct}

The file has a `2025` column with no values, so pivoting creates **263 rows of `NA`**.

<span class="foot">Remove with `drop_na()` or `values_drop_na = TRUE`.</span>
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- When you `pull(country_name)`, scroll through the list. Not every row is a country.
- The final year column is empty. Notice what `pivot_longer` does with it.
- Hand over: "Part 2, 22 minutes. Pick four countries you find interesting."
:::

## Exercises: Part 2 {.yourturn}

```{=html}
<div class="timer" data-minutes="22"></div>
```

:::: {.yt}

::: {.tasks}
[Part 2 · notebook Q1–8]{.lbl}

1. `read_csv()` the file, `rename()` column 1 to `country_name`
2. `pull()` the countries: spot the non-countries
3. `pivot_longer()` everything except `country_name`
4. `parse_number()` the `year` column
5. `filter()` four countries in 1970, 1990, 2010
6. `pivot_wider()` back to one column per year
7. `gt()` it into a formatted table
8. What have you found out?
:::

::: {.cheat}
[Syntax you need]{.lbl}

```r
lifeexp <- read_csv("data/wb-life-exp.csv") |>
  rename(country_name = 1)

lifeexp |>
  pivot_longer(-country_name, names_to = "year",
               values_to = "lifeexp") |>
  mutate(year = parse_number(year)) |>
  filter(country_name %in% c("Niger", "Honduras"),
         year %in% c(1970, 1990, 2010)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year,
              values_from = lifeexp) |>
  gt()
```

::: {.stuck}
**Stuck?**

- *does not exist in current working directory*: check the path. Is the CSV in a `data/` folder?
- Use `%in%` with a vector, not `==`
- A country returns nothing? Copy its exact spelling from `pull()`
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 22 minutes. Click the timer (or press T) to start it.

- Known issue: the notebook reads from `data/wb-life-exp.csv`. If the CSV sits next to the notebook, students need `read_csv("wb-life-exp.csv")`.
- Common errors: `==` with a vector of countries silently recycles and returns the wrong rows; country names that don't match exactly.
- Fast finishers: plot the four countries with `ggplot()` and `ggsci::scale_color_npg()`, or round with `mutate(lifeexp = round(lifeexp, 1))`.
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Debrief, 2–3 minutes.

- Ask: which countries did you pick? Who found the biggest gain, or a dip (conflict, HIV/AIDS era)?
- Point out the full pipeline. That's the shape of most of the analysis work they'll do in this course.
:::

## Iterating with `map()`

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Setup</span><span class="done">1 · dplyr</span><span class="done">2 · tidyr</span><span class="on">3 · purrr</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="flow">
  <div class="step ai"><b>A list</b><small>4 data frames</small></div><span class="arrow">→</span>
  <div class="step you"><b><code>map(list, f)</code></b><small>apply f to each element</small></div><span class="arrow">→</span>
  <div class="step ai"><b>A list</b><small>4 results</small></div>
</div>
```

::: {.cards .c2}
::: {.card}
[A function by name]{.ct}

```r
map(split_data, colnames)
```
:::

::: {.card}
[Your own steps, with `~` and `.x`]{.ct}

```r
map(split_data, ~ select(.x, author, yi, vi))
```
:::
:::

`.x` refers to the current list element.

::: {.notes}
- `map()` applies one function to every element and gives back a list of the same length.
- Two ways to write the function: a plain name, or a formula with `~` where `.x` stands for the current element.
:::

## Combining results with `bind_rows()`

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Setup</span><span class="done">1 · dplyr</span><span class="done">2 · tidyr</span><span class="on">3 · purrr</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Two steps**

```r
map(split_data,
    ~ .x |>
      as_tibble() |>
      select(author, yi, vi)) |>
  bind_rows(.id = "domain")
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**One step**

```r
map_dfr(split_data,
        ~ .x |>
          as_tibble() |>
          select(author, yi, vi),
        .id = "domain")
```
:::

::::

::: {.cards .c2}
::: {.card .dark}
[`.id = "domain"`]{.ct}
Adds a column saying which piece each row came from
:::

::: {.card .line}
[Newer purrr]{.ct}
`map_dfr()` is superseded by `map() |> list_rbind()`, but you'll still see it everywhere
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- `bind_rows` stacks the pieces. `.id` keeps track of where each row came from, so no information is lost.
- Hand over: "Part 3, 15 minutes."
:::

## Exercises: Part 3 {.yourturn}

```{=html}
<div class="timer" data-minutes="15"></div>
```

:::: {.yt}

::: {.tasks}
[Part 3 · notebook Q1–5]{.lbl}

1. Run the chunk that builds `split_data` (don't worry how it works)
2. `map()` with `head(.x, 5)`: look at each piece
3. `map()` with `colnames`, `as_tibble`, then `select()` four variables
4. Combine 3. into one `map()` with a pipe inside
5. `bind_rows(.id = "domain")` the result into one tibble
6. Bonus: do steps 4 and 5 in one go with `map_dfr()`
:::

::: {.cheat}
[Syntax you need]{.lbl}

```r
map(split_data, colnames)          # by name
map(split_data, ~ head(.x, 5))     # .x = each piece

map(split_data,
    ~ .x |>
      as_tibble() |>
      select(author, yi, vi)) |>
  bind_rows(.id = "domain")        # back to one table
```

::: {.stuck}
**Stuck?**

- *object '.x' not found*: you forgot the `~`
- `select()` fails on one piece? Each piece has different columns. Check with `map(split_data, colnames)`
- Lost track of the domain? Add `.id = "domain"`
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 15 minutes. Click the timer (or press T) to start it.

- If short of time, set the `map_dfr` bonus as homework.
- `select()` with a column that only exists in some pieces will fail: `task` is only in inhibition and shifting, `n1` only in the other two. `author`, `yi`, `vi` work everywhere.
:::
